lessonTitle: Pole Locations and the Routh Criterion

blocks.text: A hovering drone holds its altitude well at a modest controller gain. A student raises the gain to make it snappier and, above a certain value, the drone begins to bob up and down with growing amplitude until it hits the ceiling. Nothing about the hardware changed: a pair of closed-loop poles simply crossed from the left half of the s-plane to the right. Finding that gain before the flight, without computing a single root, is what the Routh criterion is for.

blocks.markdown: The poles of a linear time-invariant system are the roots of its **characteristic equation** (the denominator of the closed-loop transfer function set to zero). For a unity-feedback loop with loop transfer function $L(s)=N(s)/D(s)$ this is $1+L(s)=0$, or $D(s)+N(s)=0$. Each pole $p=\sigma+j\omega$ contributes a term $e^{\sigma t}\cos(\omega t+\phi)$ to the response, so the real part $\sigma$ (1/s) sets growth or decay and the imaginary part $\omega$ (rad/s) sets the oscillation.

rows: Simple pair on the imaginary axis ($\pm j\omega$)
blocks.caption: Pole location and the corresponding mode

blocks.title: Stability
blocks.text: A linear time-invariant system is **asymptotically stable** if every pole has a negative real part (lies strictly in the left half-plane), so every mode decays and a bounded input gives a bounded output. It is **unstable** if any pole has a positive real part. It is **marginally stable** if the poles lie in the closed left half-plane with simple roots on the imaginary axis.

blocks.markdown: **Routh-Hurwitz criterion.** Factoring a high-order polynomial by hand is hard, but the Routh array tells how many roots lie in the right half-plane without finding them. For $a_ns^n+a_{n-1}s^{n-1}+\dots+a_0=0$ with $a_n>0$, first check that all coefficients are present and positive (a necessary condition). Fill the first two rows with the coefficients taken alternately, then compute each following row from the two rows above: each entry is $(b_1a_{k+1}-a_1b_{k+1})/b_1$ with $a_1,b_1$ the leading entries of the rows above. The number of **sign changes in the first column** equals the number of roots in the right half-plane, and a polynomial is stable only if there are none.

blocks.caption: Routh array for a cubic $a_3s^3+a_2s^2+a_1s+a_0$: stable iff all $a_i>0$ and $a_2a_1>a_3a_0$.

blocks.title: Counting right-half-plane roots
blocks.prompt: How many roots of $s^4+2s^3+3s^2+4s+5=0$ lie in the right half-plane?

steps.text: All coefficients are positive, so the necessary condition holds. Rows $s^4$ and $s^3$: $[1,3,5]$ and $[2,4]$.
First column: $1,2,1,-6,5$. The sign changes are $+1\to-6$ and $-6\to+5$: two changes, so two roots in the right half-plane.
A direct root-finder confirms: the roots are $0.288\pm1.416j$ (right half-plane) and $-1.288\pm0.858j$.

blocks.answer: Two right-half-plane roots, so the system is unstable (the two growing modes oscillate at about 1.42 rad/s).

blocks.markdown: **Gain range for stability.** When a loop contains an adjustable gain $K$, the characteristic polynomial has $K$ in some coefficients. Build the Routh array symbolically and require every first-column entry to be positive; each condition gives a bound on $K$. At the limiting value an entire row becomes zero, and the **auxiliary equation** formed from the row above gives the imaginary-axis roots, which are the frequency of sustained oscillation. This shows both the largest stable $K$ and the oscillation frequency at the stability limit.

blocks.title: Range of gain for stability
blocks.prompt: A unity-feedback loop has $L(s)=\dfrac{K}{s(s+3)(s+6)}$. Find the range of $K>0$ for closed-loop stability and the oscillation frequency at the limit.

steps.text: Positivity of every entry requires $162-K>0$ and $K>0$.
At $K=162$ the $s^1$ row is zero. The auxiliary equation from the $s^2$ row is $9s^2+162=0$, so $s=\pm j\sqrt{18}=\pm4.243j$.

blocks.answer: Stable for $0<K<162$; at $K=162$ the loop oscillates steadily at $4.24$ rad/s (period 1.48 s).

blocks.title: Special cases
blocks.text: If a first-column entry is zero but the row is not all zero, replace the zero by a small positive $\epsilon$ and continue, then take the limit as $\epsilon\to0$. If an entire row is zero, use the auxiliary equation from the row above; its roots are symmetric about the origin and often lie on the imaginary axis. The test counts roots in the right half-plane, but it does not locate them, and it applies only to polynomials with real coefficients.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.text: Routh-Hurwitz gives an exact, algebraic stability limit for a gain, with no root-finding. The same boundary appears on a root locus as the imaginary-axis crossing and in a Bode plot as zero gain margin.

points: A linear system is stable when all poles lie strictly in the left half-plane; any right-half-plane pole gives a growing mode.
The Routh array's first-column sign changes equal the number of right-half-plane roots; a zero or negative coefficient already means instability or marginal stability.
For a cubic $a_3s^3+a_2s^2+a_1s+a_0$, stability needs all $a_i>0$ and $a_2a_1>a_3a_0$.
Setting the $s^1$ row of a gain-dependent array to zero gives the limiting gain, and the auxiliary equation gives the oscillation frequency.

questions.stem: Which set of closed-loop poles (in 1/s) describes a stable system?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: every pole has a strictly negative real part.
distractorRationale.b: A single pole at $+0.3$ in the right half-plane gives a slowly growing mode, so the system is unstable.
distractorRationale.c: The pole at $+1$ makes the system unstable regardless of the imaginary-axis pair.
distractorRationale.d: The complex pair has a positive real part $0.5$, so it grows.

questions.explanation: Stability requires all poles to be strictly in the left half-plane. One pole with a positive real part, however small, produces a mode $e^{\sigma t}$ that grows without bound.

questions.stem: A closed-loop system has poles at $s=-3\pm4j$. Which description of its natural response is correct?

options.text: A decaying oscillation at 4 rad/s whose envelope decays as $e^{-3t}$
A growing oscillation at 3 rad/s with envelope $e^{4t}$
Two decaying exponentials with time constants 1/3 s and 1/4 s

questions.correctOptionText: A decaying oscillation at 4 rad/s whose envelope decays as $e^{-3t}$

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the real part $-3$ sets the decay rate and the imaginary part $\pm4$ sets the oscillation frequency.
distractorRationale.b: The roles of the real and imaginary parts are swapped, and the real part is negative.
distractorRationale.c: The magnitude $5$ is $\omega_n$, not the oscillation frequency, and the real part is not zero.
distractorRationale.d: Complex poles give an oscillation, not two separate real exponentials.

questions.explanation: A pair $-\sigma\pm j\omega_d$ gives $e^{-\sigma t}\sin(\omega_dt+\phi)$. Here $\sigma=3$ s$^{-1}$ (time constant 0.33 s) and $\omega_d=4$ rad/s; the natural frequency $\omega_n=\sqrt{9+16}=5$ rad/s is larger than $\omega_d$.

questions.stem: How many roots of $s^3+2s^2+3s+10=0$ lie in the right half-plane?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the array has first column $1,2,-2,10$, with two sign changes.
distractorRationale.b: All coefficients are positive, but that is only a necessary condition; the Routh test fails here since $2\times3<1\times10$.
distractorRationale.c: Complex roots come in pairs, so a cubic with real coefficients and no real RHP root cannot have exactly one.
distractorRationale.d: If all three were in the right half-plane the first column would alternate sign each time.

questions.explanation: Row $s^1$ is $(2\cdot3-1\cdot10)/2=-2$ and row $s^0$ is $10$, giving the first column $1,2,-2,10$. The sign changes occur from $2\to-2$ and $-2\to10$, so two roots lie in the right half-plane (they are $0.22\pm2.01j$).

questions.stem: Use the Routh array to find the number of right-half-plane roots of $s^4+4s^3+6s^2+4s-15=0$. Give the count as a whole number.
questions.explanation: Rows: $s^4:[1,6,-15]$, $s^3:[4,4]$, $s^2:[(4\cdot6-4)/4,\ (4(-15))/4]=[5,-15]$, $s^1:(5\cdot4-4\cdot(-15))/5=16$, $s^0:-15$. The first column is $1,4,5,16,-15$, one sign change, so one root is in the right half-plane (at $s=1$).

questions.stem: A unity-feedback loop has $L(s)=\dfrac{K}{(s+1)(s+2)(s+3)}$. Using the Routh criterion, find the largest value of $K$ (dimensionless) for which the closed loop is stable.
questions.explanation: The characteristic equation is $(s+1)(s+2)(s+3)+K=s^3+6s^2+11s+(6+K)=0$. The cubic condition $6\times11>1\times(6+K)$ gives $K<60$. At $K=60$ the system oscillates steadily.

questions.stem: A servo loop has $L(s)=\dfrac{K}{s(s+1)(s+2)}$ with unity feedback. For what range of $K$ is it stable?

distractorRationale.b: This takes $K<$ the last coefficient of $L$ without applying the Routh condition.
distractorRationale.c: For $K>6$ two roots enter the right half-plane.
distractorRationale.d: This is the coefficient $a_2=3$, not the Routh bound $a_2a_1/a_3=6$.

questions.explanation: The characteristic polynomial is $s^3+3s^2+2s+K$. The Routh array has $s^1$ entry $(3\cdot2-K)/3$, so stability needs $0<K<6$. At $K=6$ the auxiliary equation $3s^2+6=0$ gives sustained oscillation at $\sqrt2=1.41$ rad/s.

questions.stem: A closed-loop system whose only non-left-half-plane poles are a simple pair at $s=\pm j2$ responds to a disturbance with a sustained oscillation of constant amplitude at 2 rad/s.
questions.explanation: Poles at $\pm j\omega$ produce modes $\sin\omega t$ and $\cos\omega t$ with no decay and no growth, so the system is marginally stable. Such a system is not asymptotically stable, because the oscillation never dies out.

questions.stem: For the loop $L(s)=\dfrac{K}{(s+1)(s+2)(s+3)}$ closed with unity feedback, the closed loop oscillates steadily when $K=60$. Use the auxiliary equation to find the oscillation frequency in rad/s.
questions.explanation: At $K=60$ the polynomial is $s^3+6s^2+11s+66$ and the $s^1$ row is zero. The auxiliary equation from the $s^2$ row is $6s^2+66=0$, so $s^2=-11$ and $\omega=\sqrt{11}=3.317$ rad/s. Checking: $s^3+6s^2+11s+66=(s+6)(s^2+11)$.

questions.stem: Explain how to construct a Routh array for a polynomial of order four and how to read the result. State what the necessary condition on the coefficients is, what the sign changes mean, and how special cases (a zero in the first column or a complete row of zeros) are handled.
markingGuide: Necessary condition: all coefficients present and of the same sign
First two rows from alternate coefficients; later rows from the 2-by-2 determinant formula divided by the leading entry above
Number of sign changes in the first column equals the number of right-half-plane roots
A zero in the first column is replaced by a small $\epsilon$ and the sign pattern is examined as $\epsilon\to0$
A row of zeros means an auxiliary polynomial from the row above, whose roots are symmetric about the origin and show marginal stability
questions.explanation: The Routh test is an exact counting tool and requires no root-finding. A strong answer clearly distinguishes the necessary condition (all coefficients positive) from the sufficient test of the full array.

questions.stem: A unity-feedback loop has $L(s)=\dfrac{K}{s(s+2)(s+4)}$. Determine the range of $K>0$ for closed-loop stability, the oscillation frequency at the limit, and explain what happens to the poles as $K$ increases past the limit.
markingGuide: At $K=48$ the auxiliary equation $6s^2+48=0$ gives $\omega=\sqrt8=2.83$ rad/s
For $K>48$ a complex pair moves into the right half-plane, giving a growing oscillation at about that frequency
Links the imaginary-axis crossing to the stability limit
questions.explanation: The root pair crosses the imaginary axis at $\pm2.83j$ when $K=48$, since $s^3+6s^2+8s+48=(s+6)(s^2+8)$. For larger $K$ the real part of that pair becomes positive.
